patches.new: - **Rate of natural increase (RNI)**: CBR minus CDR. Both are per 1,000 people, so the difference is also per 1,000; divide by 10 to express it as a percentage. A CBR of 30 and a CDR of 10 give a difference of 20 per 1,000, which is 2.0 per cent per year, not 20 per cent.

patches.new:
### Population Momentum

One point confuses students more than any other here: a population keeps growing for decades **after** its fertility rate has fallen to replacement level. This is **population momentum**, and it is a consequence of age structure rather than of fertility.

Think about what a country looks like at the moment its TFR reaches 2.1. The large cohorts born during its high-fertility years are still children and adolescents. They have not entered their reproductive years yet, and there are far more of them than there are elderly people at risk of dying. So even with every woman having just enough children to replace herself, the sheer number of women entering childbearing age keeps annual births above annual deaths. Growth only stops once the age structure has evened out, which takes roughly a generation or two.

Momentum is why global population is still projected to rise for most of this century even though the global TFR is already approaching replacement, and why a question that asks whether population growth stops when fertility hits 2.1 is keying “no, not for decades.”

This acceleration reflects the global spread of Stage 2 dynamics
